newsitem.title: INDIA: India in dilemma as wheat stocks fall, prices rise.
newsitem.headline: India in dilemma as wheat stocks fall, prices rise.

text.p: The Indian government is facing a grain squeeze following a poor growing season but official wheat reserves should last until until the next harvest begins in the spring, traders said on Friday.
"Reserves are falling but there should not be any significant shortage of wheat," said Tarun Kumar of Space Group, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter.
The dwindling government reserves have caused wheat prices to rise in recent months by about 20 percent compared to prices last year.
Some analysts believe growers are holding on to their stocks to further drive up prices, planning to sell their stores to the government later for a larger profit.

As of October 1, the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI) held 19.6 million tonnes of foodgrains -- which includes wheat, rice and various cereals -- down drastically from 29.9 million tonnes a year earlier.
Foodgrain stocks have fallen steadily from 25.27 million tonnes in July. They were at 32.01 million tonnes in August of 1995.
Wheat stocks fell to 11.60 million tonnes in August from 18.08 million a year earlier.
The Food Ministry has expressed hope that even if wheat procurement in the 1996/97 (July/June) season falls, it would still be possible to maintain reserves near prescribed levels on April 1, 1997.
The government has set a lower limit of 14.5 million tonnes of foodgrains, including 3.7 million tonnes of wheat and 10.8 million tonnes of rice, for April 1, 1997.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 growing season dropped sharply to 8.2 million tonnes compared to 12.3 million tonnes the previous year due to a three-million-tonne shortfall in output.
"If wheat stocks fall below four million tonnes as of early March the alarm bells will start ringing," said one Food Ministry official, who asked not to be identified.
India's new wheat crop is expected in mid-March or early April.

The Agriculture Ministry said in a report that the crop outlook for 1996/97 was excellent. It said foodgrains output is likely to reach 197 million tonnes compared to 185 million in the last growing year.
India ordered wheat exports halted in April to curb rising domestic prices and augment supplies. Traders said no wheat had been exported since September 30.

Analysts said even though government grain procurement had fallen there was still an adequate supply of wheat in the country and that the government should threaten to allow imports if farmers don't sell their grain.
"I don't think alarm bells should ring now. It is only the buffer stocks which are low. There is wheat in the country but it is not coming out," said one analyst.
"I believe the government should threaten to allow imports to get the stocks out," he said.
He said India's average annual wheat output of over 62 million tonnes in recent year was adequate in a country with such low purchasing power as India.
"Imports are a political decision. Until now there is no crisis," said Kumar.
Kumar said, however, he did not see India exporting significant amounts of wheat next year.
